knowledge_point.title: Integrating an Algebraic Function With Negative Integer Exponent

question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int (x-3)^{-8}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-3.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=1\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x-3)^{-8}\,\text{d}x & =(1)\int {u}^{-8}\cdot (1)\,\text{d}u \\  & =(1)\cdot (1)\int {u}^{-8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(1)\int {u}^{-8}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(1)\cdot \frac{{u}^{-7}}{(-7)}+C \\  & =(- \frac{1}{7})(x-3)^{-7}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{7(x-3)^{7}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{7(x-3)^{7}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{1}{7(x-3)^{7}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =(- \frac{1}{7})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(x-3)^{-7}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =(- \frac{1}{7})\cdot (-7)\cdot (x-3)^{-8}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-3)+0 \\  & =(- \frac{1}{7})\cdot (-7)\cdot (x-3)^{-8}\cdot (1) \\  & =\frac{1}{(x-3)^{8}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

generation.domain: x real; x != 3; separate primitive family on each connected interval
